lessons.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: definition, prognosis and work-up
lessons.objective: Apply the ESHRE definition (two or more losses), base prognosis on age and pregnancy history, and distinguish recommended investigations (antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid, uterus) from conditional ones (genetics, sperm DNA fragmentation) and those not recommended (inherited thrombophilia, immune and hormone panels).
lessons.closing: After two losses: antiphospholipid antibodies, TSH with TPO antibodies and the uterus; everything else only if it changes something. Inherited thrombophilia is not routinely sought, and prognosis, based on age and history, is itself an essential part of management.

lessons.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: treatment and supportive care
lessons.objective: Use aspirin plus heparin only in antiphospholipid syndrome, recognise the subgroup in which vaginal progesterone may improve live birth, explain why heparin and immunotherapies are not recommended in unexplained RPL, and give lifestyle advice and psychological support according to ESHRE.
lessons.closing: APS: aspirin before conception and heparin from the positive test. Unexplained RPL: no heparin or immunotherapy; vaginal progesterone with three or more losses and bleeding. And always: remove guilt, share the prognosis and support the next pregnancy.

lessons.title: Recurrent implantation failure: definition, work-up and interventions
lessons.objective: Apply ESHRE’s individual RIF definition with the 60% threshold, classify its investigations and interventions as recommended, to be considered or not recommended, and recognise where the RPL guideline, the add-ons document and NICE agree or differ.
lessons.closing: RIF is defined by each patient’s cumulative probability, not by a fixed number of transfers; almost all popular interventions are not recommended, and RPL recommendations do not automatically carry over to RIF.

items.title: Recurrent pregnancy loss: two losses are enough to consider it
items.core: ESHRE states that a diagnosis of recurrent pregnancy loss (RPL) could be considered after the loss of two or more pregnancies, consecutive or not. Any pregnancy confirmed by serum or urine β-hCG counts, including non-visualised (biochemical) losses, after both spontaneous conception and ART; ectopic and molar pregnancy and implantation failure are excluded. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Pregnancy loss is defined as the spontaneous demise of a pregnancy before the fetus reaches viability, that is, up to 24 weeks. Primary RPL occurs without a previous pregnancy beyond 24 weeks; secondary RPL follows one or more pregnancies that progressed beyond 24 weeks. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

The group chose two losses because it facilitates research, shared decision-making and psychological support, and allows testing for (treatable) antiphospholipid syndrome after two losses; it acknowledges that some members disagree and keep three or more consecutive losses. Prevalence is hard to estimate: about 1–2% of women with the definition of three consecutive losses before 20 weeks; according to another review, 0.8–1.4% if only clinical losses are counted and 2–3% when biochemical losses are added. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: After how many losses can RPL be considered according to ESHRE, and which types of loss are excluded from the definition?
items.pearl: Two losses open the door to investigation, but when to start each test is decided with the couple: ESHRE itself leaves it to shared decision-making and available resources.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: definition as a guideline group “conclusion” (ungraded). On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Prognosis: age and the full pregnancy history say more than any test
items.core: ESHRE recommends basing prognosis on the woman’s age and her complete pregnancy history: number of previous losses, live births and their sequence (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○). Prognostic tools such as the Kolte and Westergaard tool can be used to estimate the chance of live birth (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Women should be sensitively informed that the risk of loss is lowest between 20 and 35 years and rises rapidly after 40 (both strong). The number of previous losses is a consistent prognostic factor in cohort studies, both for the next pregnancy and in the long term. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Genetic, endocrine, anatomical and autoimmune factors together account for an estimated 50–60% of RPL, leaving 40–50% unexplained. Because no intervention has been shown to improve live birth in unexplained RPL, informing couples of their individual prognosis is itself an essential part of management. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: On which two elements does ESHRE base the prognosis of a couple with RPL?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 10 strong, ⊕⊕⊕○ (updated 2022); rec. 41 GPP (updated 2022); recs 1 and 2 strong. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: The work-up ESHRE does recommend: antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid and uterus
items.core: After two losses, ESHRE recommends testing for antiphospholipid antibodies: lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin IgG and IgM (strong); anti-β2 glycoprotein I can be considered (GPP). It recommends TSH and TPO antibodies (strong), followed by T4 if TSH is abnormal (strong), and assessment of uterine anatomy in all women (strong). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Uterus: the preferred technique is transvaginal 3D ultrasound, which distinguishes septate from bicorporeal uterus (conditional); sonohysterography is more accurate than hysterosalpingography and can be used if 3D is unavailable or tubal patency must be assessed (conditional); MRI is not first line but is a good alternative if 3D is unavailable (conditional). 2D ultrasound can be done to rule out adenomyosis (conditional, ⊕⊕○○). If a Müllerian malformation is found, investigation of the kidneys and urinary tract should be considered (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Thyroid: the rationale is the high prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism and thyroid autoimmunity in RPL. ESHRE advises against levothyroxine in euthyroid women with antibodies (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○) and to treat overt hypothyroidism (strong). Detailed thyroid management in pregnancy is beyond the scope of this module. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Which three investigations does ESHRE strongly recommend in every woman with RPL?
items.pearl: Three fronts with a strong recommendation: antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid (TSH + TPO antibodies) and uterine anatomy. Everything else is conditional or not recommended.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 15, 24, 25, 33 strong; rec. 16 GPP; recs 34–37 conditional; rec. 38 conditional, ⊕⊕○○ (new 2022); rec. 51 strong, ⊕⊕⊕○ (updated 2022); rec. 47 strong. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Genetics: pregnancy tissue analysis and parental karyotyping, not routinely
items.core: ESHRE does not routinely recommend genetic analysis of pregnancy tissue, although it could be performed for explanatory purposes (conditional); if done, it recommends array-CGH because of its reduced maternal contamination effect (strong). Parental karyotyping could be carried out after individual risk assessment, for diagnostic or explanatory purposes (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Not every couple needs testing: they should be told that even if a parental abnormality is found, cumulative live birth rates are good, and the limitations of karyotyping and the impact of its result should be explained. The probability of carrier status is very low with female age 39 or over, fewer than three losses and a negative family history. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Every couple with an abnormal fetal or parental karyotype should receive genetic counselling (GPP) and information on treatment options, with their advantages and disadvantages (GPP); the limited evidence on preimplantation genetic testing in RPL shows no clear benefit (very low quality). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Which technique does ESHRE recommend if pregnancy tissue is analysed, and why?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 11 and 13 conditional; rec. 12 strong; recs 42 and 43 GPP. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: What I would not order: inherited thrombophilia, immune panels and hormones “just in case”
items.core: ESHRE suggests not screening for inherited thrombophilia in RPL except in research or with additional risk factors for thrombophilia (conditional), because the association is absent or at best weak. ACOG also does not recommend screening for inherited thrombophilias after fetal loss (Level B), but asks to consider antiphospholipid antibodies in recurrent loss. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.body:
Immunology: ESHRE does not recommend HLA typing (conditional), anti-HY antibodies (conditional), cytokines or cytokine polymorphisms (strong) or anti-HLA antibodies (strong) in clinical practice, and considers the evidence insufficient for NK-cell testing in blood or endometrium (strong). ANA could be considered for explanatory purposes (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Endocrine and metabolic: it does not recommend testing for PCOS, fasting insulin and glucose (strong), ovarian reserve (strong), luteal phase insufficiency (strong), androgens (strong), LH (strong) or homocysteine (strong), nor prolactin without symptoms of hyperprolactinaemia (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

ACOG adds that MTHFR mutation analysis and fasting homocysteine should not be tested (Level B). [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.recall: On what do ESHRE and ACOG agree regarding inherited thrombophilia in recurrent pregnancy loss?
items.pearl: Inherited thrombophilia and antiphospholipid syndrome are not the same: the first is not routinely sought; the second is.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 17 conditional, ⊕⊕○○ (updated 2022); recs 14, 18, 21, 27 conditional; recs 19, 20, 22, 23, 26, 28–32 strong. ACOG PB 197 (2018), Level B. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: The male partner counts too: lifestyle and sperm DNA fragmentation
items.core: In RPL, ESHRE recommends assessing the male partner’s lifestyle: paternal age, smoking, alcohol, exercise and weight (strong, ⊕⊕○○). Sperm DNA fragmentation could be considered for diagnostic purposes (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○), given the growing evidence of its association with RPL. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
ESHRE notes that RPL was long considered an exclusively female problem and that possible male factors have not been adequately taken into account. For treatment, there is no evidence to support PICSI sperm selection in RPL (conditional, ⊕○○○), and antioxidants for men have not been shown to improve live birth (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Beware of applying this outside RPL: in recurrent implantation failure, the ESHRE working group does not recommend sperm DNA fragmentation or sperm FISH testing. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about sperm DNA fragmentation in RPL, and how does the implantation failure document differ?

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 39 strong, ⊕⊕○○; rec. 40 conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○; rec. 66 conditional, ⊕○○○ (all three updated 2022); rec. 67 conditional. ESHRE RIF 2023: “not recommended”. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.stem: A 31-year-old woman (fictional case) has had two non-consecutive first-trimester losses, with a child born between them. She asks whether it is “worth being investigated yet”. According to ESHRE, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Wait for a third consecutive loss, because two do not count as RPL.
options.why: ESHRE considers RPL after two losses, consecutive or not; some group members prefer three, but that is not the guideline definition.

options.text: Consider an RPL diagnosis and offer antiphospholipid antibodies, TSH with TPO antibodies and uterine assessment.
options.why: Correct: two losses are enough, and these three investigations carry a strong ESHRE recommendation.

options.text: Order an inherited thrombophilia panel (factor V Leiden, prothrombin, MTHFR).
options.why: ESHRE suggests not screening for inherited thrombophilia except with additional risk factors or in research, and ACOG advises against MTHFR testing.

options.text: Order ovarian reserve (AMH) and luteal-phase progesterone.
options.why: ESHRE recommends against testing ovarian reserve or luteal phase insufficiency in RPL (both strong).

items.explanation: The ESHRE definition includes non-consecutive losses and secondary RPL; the core work-up focuses on what can change management: antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid and uterus.

items.stem: In a couple with three early losses and no personal or family history of thrombosis, a colleague wants to order factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation and MTHFR “to start heparin if anything is positive”. Which answer fits ESHRE and ACOG?

options.text: It is reasonable: a positive result justifies prophylactic heparin to improve live birth.
options.why: ESHRE found no benefit of anticoagulation in RPL with inherited thrombophilia and suggests not using it except in research or for VTE prevention.

options.text: Only MTHFR and homocysteine make sense, as they are most associated with loss.
options.why: ACOG advises against MTHFR and fasting homocysteine testing, and ESHRE recommends against routine homocysteine measurement (strong).

options.text: Do not routinely test for inherited thrombophilia; do test for antiphospholipid antibodies.
options.why: Correct: both bodies advise against inherited thrombophilia screening in this setting and recommend (ESHRE) or ask to consider (ACOG) antiphospholipid antibodies.

options.text: Order the full panel, because guidelines recommend it from three losses.
options.why: Neither guideline recommends it by number of losses; ESHRE reserves it for research or additional risk factors.

items.explanation: The key question is whether the result changes treatment: with inherited thrombophilia, anticoagulation has not been shown to improve live birth; with antiphospholipid syndrome, there is a suggested treatment.

items.stem: A couple with two losses, the woman aged 40, no family history. They ask for “full genetic testing of both of us”. Which answer is most consistent with ESHRE?

options.text: Karyotyping of both is mandatory in all RPL.
options.why: ESHRE does not consider it routine: it is conditional and follows individual risk assessment.

options.text: With their profile the probability of carrier status is very low; karyotyping could be done after risk assessment and explaining its limitations, and even if abnormal, cumulative live birth rates are good.
options.why: Correct: it summarises the conditional recommendation and the information ESHRE asks to give.

options.text: Better to order HLA and anti-HY antibodies, which explain more losses than karyotyping.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend HLA or anti-HY antibodies in clinical practice.

options.text: If tissue is analysed after another loss, the technique of choice is conventional karyotyping by culture.
options.why: ESHRE recommends array-CGH because of its reduced maternal contamination effect (strong).

items.explanation: Parental karyotyping is not routine: it depends on individual risk and should come with information on its real usefulness and genetic counselling if abnormal.

items.title: Antiphospholipid syndrome: the only scenario for aspirin plus heparin
items.core: In women who meet the laboratory criteria for APS and have three or more losses, ESHRE suggests low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg/day) starting before conception and prophylactic-dose heparin (unfractionated or low molecular weight) starting at a positive pregnancy test, over no treatment (conditional). With two losses and APS, it suggests anticoagulation only in the context of clinical research (GPP). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
The rationale is that combined heparin and aspirin appears to improve live birth in women with APS and RPL. Testing for antiphospholipid antibodies after two losses makes sense precisely because treatment in the next pregnancy can prevent APS-associated complications. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

In inherited thrombophilia, by contrast, ESHRE found no benefit of anticoagulation and suggests not using it except in research or when indicated for VTE prevention (conditional); ACOG agrees that there is insufficient evidence for anticoagulants in RPL with inherited thrombophilia. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]
items.recall: Which regimen does ESHRE suggest for APS with three or more losses, and when does each drug start?
items.pearl: Aspirin before conception, heparin from the positive test, and only with laboratory APS and three or more losses.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 45 conditional; rec. 46 GPP; rec. 44 conditional. ACOG PB 197 (2018). On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Unexplained RPL: no heparin or aspirin; progesterone only with bleeding
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend heparin or low-dose aspirin in unexplained RPL, because there is evidence that they do not improve live birth (strong). Vaginal progesterone may improve live birth in women with three or more losses and vaginal bleeding in a subsequent pregnancy (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
In the PROMISE trial, vaginal progesterone (400 mg twice daily from soon after a positive test to 12 weeks) did not change live birth in unexplained RPL: 65.8% vs 63.3% with placebo (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.94–1.15). Combining PROMISE and PRISM, in women with at least three losses and current bleeding live birth increased (RR 1.28; 95% CI 1.08–1.51; rate difference 15%). ESHRE’s justification specifies vaginal progesterone 400 mg twice daily from presentation to 16 completed weeks. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Oral dydrogesterone started when fetal heart activity is confirmed may be effective, but more trials are needed. Outside the subgroup with three or more losses and bleeding, the 2022 guideline does not suggest progesterone: in “luteal phase insufficiency” it considers the evidence insufficient to recommend progesterone (conditional) or hCG (conditional). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: In which RPL subgroup does ESHRE suggest vaginal progesterone, and what did PROMISE show in unexplained RPL overall?
items.pearl: The indication for progesterone is defined by bleeding in the new pregnancy of a woman with three or more losses, not by the RPL diagnosis itself.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: rec. 71 strong; rec. 73 conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○ (updated 2022); recs 52 and 53 conditional. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Immunotherapies in unexplained RPL: almost all ruled out
items.core: ESHRE does not recommend lymphocyte immunisation (strong), glucocorticoids (strong), intralipid (strong, insufficient evidence) or G-CSF (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○) in unexplained RPL, and there is no evidence for endometrial scratching (GPP). The only nuanced exception is intravenous immunoglobulin. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
For intravenous immunoglobulin, ESHRE (2022) states that repeated high doses very early in pregnancy may improve live birth in women with four or more unexplained losses (conditional, ⊕⊕○○), based on a single high-quality RCT and calling for more trials. Lymphocyte immunisation may have serious adverse effects; with glucocorticoids there is some sign of benefit with prednisolone, but they are advised against because of adverse effects. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

For G-CSF, a large high-quality trial (Eapen 2019) showed no benefit and overrides the earlier smaller trial. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] Outside RPL, NICE advises against using immunological agents (intralipid, immunoglobulins or steroids) as part of fertility treatment (1.42.1). [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.recall: Which immunotherapy is the only one ESHRE leaves open in unexplained RPL, and in which subgroup?

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 68, 70, 74 strong; rec. 75 strong, ⊕⊕⊕○ and rec. 69 conditional, ⊕⊕○○ (both updated 2022); rec. 76 GPP. NICE NG257 1.42.1 [2026]. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Lifestyle and supplements: what is advised and what is not a treatment
items.core: ESHRE recommends informing couples that smoking, alcohol, obesity and excessive exercise could reduce the chance of live birth, and advising smoking cessation, normal body weight, limited alcohol and a normal exercise pattern (GPP). Obesity or being significantly underweight is associated with obstetric complications (strong). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
Low-dose folic acid is taken before conception to prevent neural tube defects, but it does not prevent loss in unexplained RPL (strong); high doses should not be used without hyperhomocysteinaemia or conditions with increased neural tube defect risk (diabetes, epilepsy). Prophylactic vitamin D may be considered in preconception counselling although evidence of effectiveness is absent (GPP), and if multivitamins are asked about, advise those safe in pregnancy (GPP), without presenting them as treatment. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Metformin in pregnancy is not recommended because of insufficient evidence in RPL with glucose metabolism defects (conditional). Stress is associated with RPL, but couples should be told there is no evidence that it directly causes loss (strong). [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: What does ESHRE say about high-dose folic acid and about the link between stress and pregnancy loss?
items.pearl: “There is no evidence that stress causes the loss” is a sentence many women need to hear explicitly.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: recs 65, 6, 8, 55, 77 GPP; recs 3, 5, 7, 72 strong; rec. 54 conditional. On the GRADE scale, ⊕⊕⊕○ = moderate quality, ⊕⊕○○ = low and ⊕○○○ = very low; strength (strong/conditional) and quality are different things. ⊕ symbols are given only for recommendations updated in 2022 (HRO summary article); for the others they could not be read in our copy of the PDF and are not stated.

items.title: Supportive care: listen, avoid false reassurance and support the next pregnancy
items.core: ESHRE describes pregnancy loss as a significant negative life event whose repetitive nature may intensify grief, and asks clinicians and clinics to take the couple’s psychosocial needs into account when organising care. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.body:
There is no single model, but the guideline lists valued elements: recognising the patient as an individual, time for questions and repetition, listening to facts and feelings, respect for the couple and the lost pregnancies, clear and sensitive language (avoiding terms such as “recurrent abortion”, “products of conception” or “blighted ovum”, and mirroring the patient’s terms), honesty without false reassurance, shared planning, access to the team and early scans if wanted in the next pregnancy, and kindness. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

In one study, the odds of moderate to severe depression were more than five times higher in women with RPL; studies focus on women and data on the impact on men are lacking, and their support preferences may differ. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Name four elements of supportive care that ESHRE considers valuable in RPL.
items.pearl: Useful phrase: “There is no evidence that stress caused what happened, and it is not your fault; let us plan the next pregnancy together.”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022: guideline group “conclusion” on psychosocial needs (ungraded); supportive care elements as guideline text, not a graded recommendation.

items.stem: A 35-year-old woman with three unexplained losses is now 7 weeks pregnant with light vaginal bleeding. What fits ESHRE 2022?

options.text: Vaginal progesterone, 400 mg twice daily, up to 16 completed weeks.
options.why: Correct: with three or more losses and bleeding, ESHRE suggests vaginal progesterone (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○), and its justification specifies this regimen.

options.text: Low molecular weight heparin plus aspirin, because it is RPL.
options.why: In unexplained RPL, ESHRE does not recommend heparin or aspirin (strong).

options.text: Prednisolone, because there are signs of benefit in selected women.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend glucocorticoids in unexplained RPL because of adverse effects (strong).

options.text: Nothing: PROMISE showed progesterone is useless in every woman with RPL.
options.why: PROMISE was neutral in unexplained RPL overall, but the combined analysis with PRISM showed benefit with three or more losses and bleeding.

items.explanation: The subgroup with benefit is women with at least three losses and bleeding in the current pregnancy (RR 1.28 in the combined analysis).

items.stem: A woman with three losses and persistently positive lupus anticoagulant (meets APS laboratory criteria), with no previous thrombosis. What does ESHRE suggest?

options.text: Therapeutic-dose heparin from before conception.
options.why: ESHRE suggests prophylactic-dose heparin starting at a positive pregnancy test.

options.text: Low-dose aspirin (75–100 mg/day) from before conception and prophylactic heparin from the positive test.
options.why: Correct: this is the suggested regimen (conditional) for laboratory APS with three or more losses.

options.text: Aspirin only; heparin is reserved for APS with two losses.
options.why: With two losses and APS, ESHRE suggests anticoagulation only in research (GPP); with three or more it suggests the combination.

options.text: High-dose intravenous immunoglobulin.
options.why: The guideline does not propose immunoglobulin for APS; its comment on them refers to four or more unexplained losses.

items.explanation: APS is the scenario where aspirin + heparin has support; unexplained RPL is not.

items.stem: A patient with three unexplained losses brings a proposal from another clinic: blood NK-cell testing and, if high, intralipid and G-CSF. Which answer is consistent with ESHRE?

options.text: Accept: high NK cells identify who to treat with immunotherapy.
options.why: ESHRE states that NK-cell testing cannot be used to select women for immunological treatments.

options.text: Accept only G-CSF, which has a positive trial.
options.why: The large Eapen trial (2019) showed no benefit and overrides the earlier one; ESHRE does not recommend it (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○).

options.text: Advise against NK testing, intralipid and G-CSF, and explain prognosis based on age and pregnancy history.
options.why: Correct: all three have strong recommendations against or for insufficient evidence, and individual prognosis is an essential part of management.

options.text: Replace it with steroids, which are cheaper.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend glucocorticoids in unexplained RPL (strong).

items.explanation: In unexplained RPL there are no immune tests that guide effective treatment; honestly sharing the individual prognosis (often good) is an essential part of management.

items.stem: After her second loss, a patient asks whether it was caused by work stress and whether she should take 5 mg folic acid. She has no diabetes, epilepsy or hyperhomocysteinaemia. What would you tell her according to ESHRE?

options.text: That stress is associated with RPL but there is no evidence it causes it, and to take low-dose folic acid to prevent neural tube defects, not high doses.
options.why: Correct: that there is no evidence stress causes loss and that low-dose folic acid does not prevent it are strong ESHRE recommendations; avoiding high doses without an indication is stated in the justification of the latter.

options.text: That stress is the most likely cause and she should take sick leave.
options.why: ESHRE asks to inform that there is no evidence that stress directly causes loss.

options.text: That she should take 5 mg folic acid because it prevents further losses.
options.why: Folic acid has not been shown to prevent loss, and ESHRE advises against high doses without an indication.

options.text: That she should have her vitamin D measured, because it explains many losses.
options.why: ESHRE only suggests considering prophylactic vitamin D in preconception counselling (GPP), with no evidence of effectiveness against loss.

items.explanation: Removing guilt and avoiding unnecessary supplements are two messages backed by strong ESHRE recommendations (the high-dose point in its justification).

items.title: Case: Sofía, Joaquín and three unexplained losses

steps.text: Sofía (fictional case), 34, and Joaquín, 38, have had two first-trimester losses. Sofía asks whether they need to wait for a third before being investigated. ESHRE considers RPL after two losses and recommends testing for antiphospholipid antibodies, thyroid function and uterine anatomy. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Before the results arrive, Sofía has a third loss. A relative recommends an inherited thrombophilia panel. They are told that neither ESHRE nor ACOG recommends it routinely in this setting and that anticoagulation has not shown benefit in inherited thrombophilia. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] [[ref:acog-2018-pb197-thrombophilia]]

Antiphospholipid antibodies negative, TSH and TPO antibodies normal, 3D ultrasound normal. Joaquín smokes; his lifestyle is reviewed, as ESHRE recommends, and he is advised to stop smoking. They are told that prognosis is based on age and pregnancy history, and that a substantial share of RPL remains unexplained. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Sofía asks whether she should take heparin and aspirin “just in case” in the next pregnancy. In unexplained RPL, ESHRE does not recommend them because they do not improve live birth. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

Months later, Sofía is 7 weeks pregnant and presents with light bleeding. With three previous losses and current bleeding, ESHRE suggests vaginal progesterone. The support the couple wants is arranged, with access to the team and early scans. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]

items.title: Recurrent implantation failure: an individual definition with a 60% threshold
items.core: The ESHRE working group considers recurrent implantation failure (RIF) a secondary phenomenon of ART: the transfer of embryos considered viable has failed to result in a positive pregnancy test sufficiently often, in a specific patient, to warrant consideration of further investigations or interventions. The recommended threshold is a cumulative predicted chance of implantation of 60%. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.body:
If implantation has not occurred after a number of transfers whose cumulative predicted chance exceeds 60%, counselling on investigations or treatment should be offered; if that threshold has not yet been reached, simply proceeding to another cycle is indicated. This avoids a fixed number of transfers for everyone. To approximate the chance after n transfers it proposes 1 − (1 − PR)ⁿ, where PR is the pregnancy rate per transfer (which can be estimated by multiplying the live birth rate by 1.16); the model should consider at least age, euploidy if screened, and the number of cleavage-stage embryos or blastocysts transferred. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

The 95% threshold proposed by other authors would be useful for research, but very few patients reach it. A standard fertility work-up before ART is assumed. ESHRE explicitly excludes implantation failure from the RPL definition. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]]
items.recall: Which cumulative probability threshold does ESHRE propose to define RIF, and which formula does it suggest to estimate it?
items.pearl: Arithmetic example: with a 35% pregnancy rate per transfer, two transfers add up to 1 − 0.65² ≈ 58% (not yet RIF) and three to 1 − 0.65³ ≈ 73% (now it is).

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE Working Group on RIF 2023 (Hum Reprod Open), definition and threshold. Good practice document (expert opinion supported by the literature), without GRADE ratings: each test or intervention is classed as recommended, to be considered, or not recommended (not to be offered routinely). The 35% example is our own illustrative calculation with the document’s formula, not a figure from the source.

items.title: RIF work-up: what is recommended, what can be considered and what is not
items.core: Recommended: review and optimise lifestyle in both partners, re-assess endometrial thickness (and review the estradiol regimen if it remains thin) and, if a chromosomal abnormality is detected, genetic counselling and PGT where relevant; antiphospholipid antibodies are recommended when there are additional risk factors for thrombophilia. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.body:
Can be considered: karyotyping of both partners (despite the low prevalence), 3D ultrasound if not done before, hysteroscopy (especially if ultrasound suggests an anomaly), HSG or other tubal imaging if hydrosalpinx is in doubt, assessment for chronic endometritis with antibiotics if diagnosed, specific aspects of endometrial function, thyroid function, late follicular and mid-luteal progesterone, and antiphospholipid antibodies without risk factors. There are insufficient data to recommend routine use of any commercial endometrial receptivity test, or measuring or treating vitamin D. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Not recommended: uterine or vaginal microbiome profiling, peripheral or uterine NK cells, uterine T lymphocytes, blood cytokines, HLA-C compatibility, embryo mitochondrial DNA, sperm FISH and sperm DNA fragmentation. On thrombophilia, the role of testing would be very limited and focused on a personal or family history of thrombosis. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.recall: List three recommended, three to-be-considered and three not-recommended investigations in RIF according to ESHRE.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE Working Group on RIF 2023: 19 recommendations on investigations. Good practice document (expert opinion supported by the literature), without GRADE ratings: each test or intervention is classed as recommended, to be considered, or not recommended (not to be offered routinely). The colour-coded summary figures are images not included in our text; the table wording is cited.

items.title: Interventions for RIF: almost everything “not recommended”
items.core: The ESHRE working group does not recommend intentional endometrial injury (scratching), G-CSF, intralipid, intravenous immunoglobulin, intrauterine PBMC, PRP or hCG infusion, low molecular weight heparin, GnRH agonist or aromatase inhibitor pre-treatment, or assisted hatching for RIF. It only considers PGT-A and blastocyst-stage transfer. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.body:
Heparin in RIF (three or more failed transfers) did not improve live birth in a meta-analysis of 2 RCTs with 71 patients (RR 1.38; 95% CI 0.64–2.96). For PGT-A, the meta-analysis of RCTs in RIF showed no increase in live birth (RR 0.98; 95% CI 0.32–2.94), although retrospective studies using current techniques suggest it reduces the number of transfers needed. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

The document stresses that many interventions are applied empirically under pressure to act, and that if a cause is identified (thyroid dysfunction, APS, uterine malformation, endometriosis or adenomyosis), the relevant guideline should be followed. For some couples gamete donation may be an option, although studies confirming that it improves outcomes after RIF are lacking. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.recall: Which two interventions does ESHRE only say “can be considered” in RIF, and what does it say about heparin?
items.pearl: In RIF, the “no” list is much longer than the “yes” list: the most useful step is often to recalculate the prognosis and carry on.

evidence.label: not-recommended
evidence.note: ESHRE Working Group on RIF 2023: recommendations on interventions. Good practice document (expert opinion supported by the literature), without GRADE ratings: each test or intervention is classed as recommended, to be considered, or not recommended (not to be offered routinely).

items.title: RPL, RIF and add-ons: where the documents agree and where they differ
items.core: The RIF document, the add-ons document and NICE agree on not using immunotherapy or immune testing: the add-ons document does not recommend peripheral blood immune tests or uterine NK testing, and NICE advises against immunological agents in fertility treatment (1.42.1); the RPL guideline is the partial exception, because of immunoglobulin. They differ on PGT-A: the RIF document considers it, whereas the add-ons document does not recommend it routinely and NICE advises against offering it to improve live birth (1.48.1). [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]] [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:nice-2026-ng257]]
items.body:
Sperm DNA fragmentation: can be considered in RPL (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○), but is not recommended in RIF. Immunoglobulin: the RPL guideline leaves open a possible improvement with four or more unexplained losses (conditional), whereas the RIF document does not recommend it. Antiphospholipid antibodies: recommended after two losses in RPL (strong); in RIF, recommended with risk factors and to be considered without them. Thyroid: TSH and TPO antibodies recommended in RPL (strong); in RIF, only to be considered. [[ref:eshre-2022-rpl]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]

Hysteroscopy: the add-ons document does not recommend routine screening hysteroscopy, but considers it in RIF, in line with the RIF document. [[ref:eshre-2023-addons]] [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.recall: Name two points on which the ESHRE RPL guideline and RIF document do not say the same thing.
items.pearl: Before applying a recommendation, check which population it refers to: RPL (losses after a confirmed pregnancy) and RIF (no positive test after transfers) are not interchangeable.

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE 2022 RPL: rec. 40 conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○; rec. 69 conditional, ⊕⊕○○; recs 15 and 24 strong. ESHRE RIF 2023 (good practice). ESHRE add-ons 2023 (own four-phrase scale). NICE NG257 1.42.1 and 1.48.1 [2026].

items.title: Supporting RIF: honesty about the evidence and data-based hope
items.core: The RIF document adapts the supportive care elements of the RPL guideline and insists on being honest about the evidence, or lack of benefit, for investigations and treatments offered without solid grounds. According to a study it cites, half of patients with RIF achieve a live birth with ART within 5 years. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.body: Women with RIF report more stress than fertile controls, social isolation and lower hope after repeated cycles; there are no data on male partners. Couples can be reassured with their individual estimate of implantation in the next cycle, and the document cites the suggestion that planning several cycles from the start, anticipating failure and how to cope with it, could be beneficial. [[ref:eshre-2023-rif]]
items.recall: Which prognostic figure does the RIF document cite to give the couple realistic hope?
items.pearl: Useful phrase: “With your data, continuing with transfers is a reasonable option; let me explain which tests make sense and which have not been shown to help.”

evidence.label: guideline
evidence.note: ESHRE Working Group on RIF 2023, patient care and counselling section (text, not a graded recommendation).

items.stem: A couple whose clinic model gives them a 30% pregnancy rate per transfer have had two transfers without a positive test and ask for “the implantation failure work-up”. Using the ESHRE document formula (1 − (1 − PR)ⁿ), what is most appropriate?

options.text: It is already RIF: two failed transfers are enough.
options.why: The document avoids a fixed number of transfers and uses individual cumulative probability.

options.text: Their cumulative probability is 1 − 0.7² = 51%, below 60%: another transfer is indicated.
options.why: Correct: they have not reached the threshold, so the document advises simply proceeding to another cycle.

options.text: They must wait to exceed 95%.
options.why: The 95% is mentioned as a research threshold; the recommended clinical one is 60%.

options.text: Their cumulative probability is 60% (30% + 30%): it is already RIF.
options.why: Probabilities do not add up: with the formula, two transfers at 30% give 51%.

items.explanation: With 30% per transfer, a third transfer takes the cumulative probability to 1 − 0.7³ ≈ 66%; if it failed, it would exceed 60%. (Illustrative calculation with the document’s formula.)

items.stem: A woman with confirmed RIF, no history of thrombosis and negative antiphospholipid antibodies has been offered low molecular weight heparin, intrauterine PRP and immunoglobulin. What does ESHRE say?

options.text: All three are “not recommended” in RIF.
options.why: Correct: the RIF document does not recommend heparin to increase pregnancy or live birth, intrauterine PRP or immunoglobulin.

options.text: Heparin is recommended in all RIF; the other two are not.
options.why: The cited meta-analysis showed no effect of heparin on live birth in RIF.

options.text: PRP “can be considered” because it increased clinical pregnancy.
options.why: Intrauterine PRP infusion is classed as not recommended in RIF.

options.text: Immunoglobulin is recommended after four or more failures.
options.why: That nuance (four or more losses) belongs to the RPL guideline, not RIF, and is conditional there; in RIF it is not recommended.

items.explanation: What is suggested for RPL should not be transferred to RIF: they are different populations with different recommendations.

items.stem: In a couple with RIF, which of these tests is classed as “can be considered” by the ESHRE working group?

options.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation.
options.why: In RIF, sperm DNA fragmentation and sperm FISH are not recommended.

options.text: Peripheral blood NK cells.
options.why: Peripheral (and uterine) NK-cell testing is not recommended.

options.text: Assessment for chronic endometritis, with antibiotics if diagnosed.
options.why: Correct: both “can be considered” in the RIF document.

options.text: Uterine and vaginal microbiome profiling.
options.why: Microbiome profiling is not recommended.

items.explanation: In RIF few tests are “recommended”; several can be considered case by case, and many of the most popular are not recommended.

items.stem: According to ESHRE (2022), which pregnancies count towards a diagnosis of recurrent pregnancy loss?

options.text: Any β-hCG-confirmed pregnancy, including biochemical and ART ones; not ectopic or molar pregnancies, nor implantation failure.
options.why: Correct: this is how ESHRE defines the pregnancies that count.

options.text: Only ultrasound-confirmed, spontaneous intrauterine losses, not counting biochemical ones or those after ART.
options.why: Non-visualised (biochemical) losses and those after ART also count.

options.text: Any β-hCG-confirmed pregnancy, including ectopic and molar ones, provided the losses were consecutive.
options.why: Ectopic and molar pregnancies are excluded, and losses need not be consecutive.

options.text: Clinical losses and implantation failures after transfer, because both reflect the same problem.
options.why: ESHRE expressly excludes implantation failure from the definition of RPL.

items.explanation: ESHRE states that the diagnosis can be considered after two or more losses, consecutive or not.

items.stem: A woman (fictional case) had a birth at 38 weeks and then two first-trimester losses. How is this classified according to ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: Primary RPL, because both losses occurred after the birth and are the only ones that count.
options.why: Primary RPL is that occurring without a previous pregnancy beyond 24 weeks.

options.text: Not RPL, because a previous term birth excludes the diagnosis even with two losses.
options.why: A previous birth does not exclude the diagnosis: it defines secondary RPL.

options.text: Not yet RPL, because ESHRE requires three consecutive losses before 20 weeks.
options.why: ESHRE accepts the diagnosis after two losses, consecutive or not; three consecutive is the definition others keep.

options.text: Secondary RPL, because there was at least one previous pregnancy beyond 24 weeks.
options.why: Correct: secondary RPL occurs after one or more pregnancies beyond 24 weeks.

items.explanation: ESHRE defines pregnancy loss as spontaneous demise of a pregnancy before viability, that is, up to 24 weeks.

items.stem: Why did ESHRE (2022) choose two losses, rather than three, as the threshold to consider RPL?

options.text: Because it eases research, shared decision-making and support, and allows APS testing; some members disagree.
options.why: Correct: the group acknowledges that some of its members keep three or more consecutive losses.

options.text: Because RCTs showed that treating after two losses increases live birth compared with waiting for the third.
options.why: The guideline does not base the threshold on treatment RCTs, but on practical reasons and APS testing.

options.text: Because prevalence with two losses is identical to that with three, so the threshold changes nothing.
options.why: Prevalence varies greatly with the definition; with three consecutive losses it is around 1–2%.

options.text: Because after two losses a genetic cause is certain and karyotyping of every couple is indicated.
options.why: ESHRE does not consider karyotyping of every couple indicated; it depends on individual risk.

items.explanation: The timing of each test is decided with the couple: ESHRE itself leaves it to shared decision-making and available resources.

items.stem: According to ESHRE (2022), what should the prognosis of a woman with RPL be based on?

options.text: On the karyotype of both partners and genetic analysis of each loss.
options.why: Neither karyotyping nor tissue analysis is recommended routinely, and they are not the basis of prognosis.

options.text: On anti-Müllerian hormone and antral follicle count, as markers of oocyte quality.
options.why: ESHRE does not recommend ovarian reserve testing in RPL (strong).

options.text: On the woman's age and full pregnancy history: losses, live births and their sequence.
options.why: Correct: strong recommendation, ⊕⊕⊕○; tools such as Kolte and Westergaard's can help (GPP).

options.text: On the peripheral blood NK cell count, which predicts the next loss.
options.why: ESHRE considers the evidence insufficient for NK cell testing (strong).

items.explanation: The number of previous losses is a consistent prognostic factor in cohort studies, both for the next pregnancy and in the long term.

items.stem: What proportion of RPL do genetic, endocrine, anatomical and autoimmune factors explain together, according to ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: About 90%, so unexplained RPL is a rarity after a complete work-up.
options.why: Invented figure: 40–50% of RPL remains unexplained.

options.text: About 10%, because almost all RPL is due to sporadic embryonic aneuploidy.
options.why: Invented figure: these factors explain 50–60%.

options.text: 50–60%; the remaining 40–50% stays unexplained.
options.why: Correct: that is why counselling on individual prognosis is an essential part of management.

options.text: 25%; the rest is attributed to untested inherited thrombophilias.
options.why: Invented figure, and the association with inherited thrombophilia is absent or weak.

items.explanation: As no intervention has been shown to improve live birth in unexplained RPL, individual prognosis is itself part of management.

items.stem: A 42-year-old woman and a 28-year-old woman (fictional cases), both with two losses, ask about their risk. What does ESHRE (2022) say about age?

options.text: That age does not influence the risk of loss once RPL is diagnosed.
options.why: Age is one of the two pillars of prognosis.

options.text: That the risk of loss is lowest between 20 and 35 years and rises rapidly after 40.
options.why: Correct: both statements are strong recommendations to be communicated sensitively.

options.text: That the risk increases linearly from age 20, with no relevant change after 40.
options.why: ESHRE describes the lowest risk between 20 and 35 and a rapid rise after 40.

options.text: That the risk is highest before age 25, owing to endometrial immaturity, and stabilises afterwards.
options.why: Invented claim that contradicts the guideline.

items.explanation: ESHRE asks for these data to be communicated sensitively, together with the full pregnancy history.

items.stem: Which antiphospholipid antibody testing does ESHRE (2022) recommend after two losses?

options.text: Only anti-β2-glycoprotein I, because lupus anticoagulant gives too many false positives during the work-up.
options.why: Lupus anticoagulant is part of what is recommended; anti-β2-GPI can only be considered (GPP).

options.text: Lupus anticoagulant and anticardiolipin IgG and IgM (strong); anti-β2-glycoprotein I can be considered (GPP).
options.why: Correct: this is the combination recommended by the guideline.

options.text: None until the third loss, because antiphospholipid syndrome is only treated from three losses onwards.
options.why: Testing after two losses makes sense precisely because treatment can prevent complications.

options.text: Anticardiolipin IgA and antinuclear antibodies, as an initial autoimmunity screen in all women.
options.why: The strong recommendation is anticardiolipin IgG and IgM with lupus anticoagulant; ANA can only be considered for explanatory purposes.

items.explanation: Antiphospholipids, thyroid (TSH and anti-TPO) and uterine anatomy are the three areas with strong recommendations.

items.stem: To assess uterine anatomy in RPL, which technique does ESHRE (2022) prefer?

options.text: Hysterosalpingography, being more accurate than sonohysterography for Müllerian anomalies.
options.why: It is the other way round: sonohysterography is more accurate than hysterosalpingography.

options.text: MRI as first line in all women, given its higher resolution than ultrasound.
options.why: MRI is not first line; it is a good alternative if 3D ultrasound is unavailable.

options.text: Diagnostic hysteroscopy in all women, because ultrasound cannot identify a septum.
options.why: 3D ultrasound distinguishes a septate from a bicorporeal uterus.

options.text: 3D transvaginal ultrasound, which distinguishes a septate from a bicorporeal uterus (conditional).
options.why: Correct: assessing the uterus in all women is strong; the choice of technique is conditional.

items.explanation: With a Müllerian malformation, renal and urinary tract assessment should be considered (conditional), and 2D ultrasound can be done to rule out adenomyosis (conditional, ⊕⊕○○).

items.stem: A woman with two losses (fictional case) has normal TSH and positive anti-TPO. What does ESHRE (2022) say?

options.text: Do not treat a euthyroid woman with antibodies with levothyroxine (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○).
options.why: Correct: overt hypothyroidism is treated (strong).

options.text: Start low-dose levothyroxine before conception to reduce the next loss.
options.why: ESHRE recommends not treating a euthyroid woman with antibodies.

options.text: Repeat anti-TPO monthly and treat only if the titre keeps rising in pregnancy.
options.why: The guideline does not propose this titre-monitoring strategy.

options.text: Add low-dose corticosteroids, because thyroid autoimmunity indicates an immune cause.
options.why: Glucocorticoids are not recommended in unexplained RPL (strong).

items.explanation: TSH and anti-TPO are requested because of the high prevalence of subclinical hypothyroidism and thyroid autoimmunity in RPL, with T4 if TSH is abnormal.

items.stem: If genetic analysis of pregnancy tissue is decided on, which technique does ESHRE (2022) recommend and why?

options.text: Conventional culture karyotyping, as it is the only one that detects balanced translocations in the tissue.
options.why: The strong recommendation is array-CGH, given its lower maternal contamination effect.

options.text: Whole-exome sequencing, because it identifies the monogenic cause in most losses.
options.why: The guideline does not recommend this technique and the claim about most losses is invented.

options.text: Array-CGH (strong), because of its lower maternal contamination effect; the analysis is not recommended routinely.
options.why: Correct: it can be done for explanatory purposes (conditional) and, if done, with array-CGH.

options.text: FISH for chromosomes 13, 18, 21, X and Y, being the cheapest and sufficient for prognosis.
options.why: This is not the technique recommended by the guideline.

items.explanation: Analysis of pregnancy tissue is not recommended routinely, but can be done for explanatory purposes (conditional).

items.stem: In a couple with RPL (fictional case), the man carries a balanced translocation. According to ESHRE (2022), what is most appropriate?

options.text: Indicate PGT as the only option, as it has clearly been shown to increase live birth in RPL.
options.why: The scarce evidence on preimplantation genetic diagnosis in RPL shows no clear benefit (very low quality).

options.text: Genetic counselling and information on options, with their advantages and disadvantages (GPP).
options.why: Correct: it also helps to know that cumulative live birth rates are good even if one partner is a carrier.

options.text: Advise against further spontaneous pregnancies and refer directly for gamete donation.
options.why: The guideline does not say so; cumulative live birth rates are good even if one parent is a carrier.

options.text: Repeat both karyotypes yearly and make no decisions until stability is confirmed.
options.why: This has no basis in the guideline: a constitutional karyotype does not need repeating.

items.explanation: Every couple with an abnormal fetal or parental karyotype should receive genetic counselling and information on treatment options (both GPP).

items.stem: On inherited thrombophilia in recurrent loss, which statement correctly reflects ESHRE (2022) and ACOG (PB 197)?

options.text: ESHRE recommends testing after three losses (strong); ACOG already after two losses, together with MTHFR.
options.why: Neither recommends routine testing, and ACOG says not to test MTHFR (level B).

options.text: ESHRE does not address it; ACOG recommends inherited thrombophilia screening after fetal losses.
options.why: ESHRE does address it (conditional) and ACOG does not recommend that screening (level B).

options.text: Both recommend testing if antiphospholipids are negative, to decide whether to use heparin in pregnancy.
options.why: Neither recommends it for that purpose; no benefit of anticoagulation was found in inherited thrombophilia.

options.text: ESHRE: do not test except in research or with added risk (conditional); ACOG: do not screen after fetal loss (level B).
options.why: Correct: ACOG adds that MTHFR and fasting homocysteine should not be tested (level B).

items.explanation: The association between inherited thrombophilia and RPL is absent or, at most, weak; antiphospholipid antibodies should be tested.

items.stem: In RPL, which of these immunological tests can be considered according to ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: HLA typing of both partners, to assess compatibility.
options.why: HLA typing is not recommended in clinical practice (conditional).

options.text: NK cells in blood or endometrium, to decide on immunotherapy.
options.why: ESHRE considers the evidence insufficient for NK testing (strong).

options.text: Antinuclear antibodies (ANA), for explanatory purposes.
options.why: Correct: ANA can be considered for explanatory purposes (conditional).

options.text: Cytokines and their polymorphisms, to choose treatment.
options.why: They are not recommended (strong).

items.explanation: Anti-HY antibodies (conditional) and anti-HLA antibodies (strong) are not recommended either.

items.stem: In the endocrine work-up of RPL, which statement matches ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: It recommends AMH and luteal-phase progesterone in all women, to detect low reserve and luteal insufficiency.
options.why: It does not recommend testing ovarian reserve or luteal insufficiency (both strong).

options.text: It does not recommend ovarian reserve, androgens, LH or homocysteine (strong), nor prolactin without symptoms (conditional).
options.why: Correct: prolactin is only advised against when there are no clinical signs of hyperprolactinaemia.

options.text: It recommends fasting insulin and glucose in all women, because PCOS is the main endocrine cause.
options.why: It does not recommend testing for PCOS, insulin or fasting glucose (strong).

options.text: It recommends fasting homocysteine and MTHFR, to indicate high-dose folic acid if abnormal.
options.why: It does not recommend homocysteine (strong); ACOG does not recommend MTHFR or homocysteine either (level B).

items.explanation: Of the endocrine work-up, ESHRE strongly recommends only TSH and anti-TPO (with T4 if TSH is abnormal).

items.stem: What does ESHRE (2022) recommend on assessing the male partner in RPL?

options.text: Nothing: RPL is an exclusively female problem and the man needs no specific assessment.
options.why: ESHRE criticises precisely this view and recommends assessing the man.

options.text: Semen analysis, sperm FISH and routine karyotyping in all men of couples with RPL (strong).
options.why: This is not what the guideline recommends; karyotyping depends on individual risk.

options.text: Sperm DNA fragmentation in all men (strong) and antioxidants for three months if elevated.
options.why: Fragmentation can only be considered (conditional) and antioxidants have not been shown to improve live birth.

options.text: Assess his lifestyle (strong, ⊕⊕○○); sperm DNA fragmentation can be considered (conditional).
options.why: Correct: paternal age, smoking, alcohol, exercise and weight; fragmentation, conditional ⊕⊕⊕○.

items.explanation: ESHRE notes that possible male factors were not sufficiently considered for a long time.

items.stem: The male partner in a couple with RPL (fictional case) asks about PICSI sperm selection and taking antioxidants. What does ESHRE (2022) say?

options.text: There is no evidence supporting PICSI (conditional, ⊕○○○) and antioxidants have not improved live birth.
options.why: Correct: both recommendations are conditional.

options.text: PICSI is recommended if fragmentation is high, and antioxidants for three months before conception.
options.why: The guideline recommends neither; the three-month regimen is invented.

options.text: Antioxidants improve live birth (strong) and PICSI has not yet been studied in couples with RPL.
options.why: Antioxidants have not been shown to improve live birth, and the guideline does address PICSI.

options.text: PICSI can be considered (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○) and antioxidants only if the man smokes or is overweight.
options.why: The recommendation on PICSI is that there is no evidence to support it (⊕○○○).

items.explanation: Assessing the man is not the same as treating him with add-ons: what is recommended is reviewing his lifestyle.

items.stem: A woman with two losses (fictional case) meets laboratory criteria for APS and has no history of thrombosis. What does ESHRE (2022) say about anticoagulation?

options.text: Therapeutic-dose heparin from before conception, as APS is confirmed.
options.why: The regimen the guideline suggests with three or more losses is prophylactic heparin from the positive test, not preconception therapeutic dosing.

options.text: Aspirin alone, and heparin only after a third loss, with no other considerations.
options.why: With two losses, the guideline does not suggest aspirin alone; it suggests anticoagulation only within research (GPP).

options.text: Anticoagulate only within clinical research (GPP); the combined regimen is suggested with three or more losses.
options.why: Correct: aspirin and heparin are suggested over no treatment with three or more losses (conditional).

options.text: The same regimen as with three losses (strong), as the guideline does not distinguish the number of losses in APS.
options.why: The guideline does distinguish: with three or more, conditional; with two, only in research (GPP).

items.explanation: Testing antiphospholipids after two losses makes sense because treatment in the next pregnancy may prevent APS-related complications.

items.stem: A woman with RPL was diagnosed with heterozygous factor V Leiden at another clinic (fictional case), with no history of thrombosis. What do ESHRE and ACOG say about anticoagulating her to prevent loss?

options.text: ESHRE: do not anticoagulate except in research or for thromboembolism prevention (conditional); ACOG: insufficient evidence.
options.why: Correct: neither supports anticoagulation to prevent loss in this scenario.

options.text: Both recommend aspirin and prophylactic heparin from the positive test, just as in antiphospholipid syndrome.
options.why: The combined regimen is reserved for APS; no benefit was found in inherited thrombophilia.

options.text: ESHRE recommends therapeutic-dose heparin (strong); ACOG only low-dose aspirin from week 12.
options.why: Neither recommends those regimens to prevent loss.

options.text: ESHRE does not address this scenario; ACOG recommends prophylactic heparin with two or more losses.
options.why: ESHRE does address it (conditional) and ACOG considers the evidence insufficient.

items.explanation: An indication for venous thromboembolism prevention is assessed on its own merits; it is not a treatment for RPL.

items.stem: In the PROMISE trial (unexplained RPL), live birth was 65.8% with vaginal progesterone and 63.3% with placebo (RR 1.04; 95% CI 0.94–1.15). Combining PROMISE and PRISM, in women with at least three losses and current bleeding it was RR 1.28 (95% CI 1.08–1.51). What is concluded?

options.text: That progesterone benefits every woman with unexplained RPL, because both RRs are above 1.
options.why: In PROMISE the interval includes 1: there was no effect in unexplained RPL overall.

options.text: That progesterone is useless in every subgroup, because the main trial was negative.
options.why: In the subgroup with three or more losses and bleeding the interval does not include 1.

options.text: That the benefit is limited to women with two previous losses and no bleeding in the current pregnancy.
options.why: It is the reverse: the benefit was seen with at least three losses and current bleeding.

options.text: That there was no effect in unexplained RPL overall, but there was with three or more losses and current bleeding.
options.why: Correct: ESHRE translates this into a conditional recommendation (⊕⊕⊕○) for that subgroup.

items.explanation: The indication is defined by bleeding in the new pregnancy of a woman with three or more losses, not by the RPL diagnosis.

items.stem: A woman with three unexplained losses (fictional case) is 6 weeks pregnant, without bleeding, and asks for aspirin, heparin and progesterone “just in case”. What matches ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: All three, because in unexplained RPL the combination has been shown to improve live birth.
options.why: Heparin and aspirin are not recommended in unexplained RPL (strong), and there is no evidence for that combination.

options.text: Neither heparin nor aspirin (strong); progesterone is suggested if bleeding occurs in this pregnancy.
options.why: Correct: vaginal progesterone is suggested with three or more losses and bleeding (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○).

options.text: Aspirin only, because it is harmless and the guideline suggests it in all RPL from before conception.
options.why: Preconception aspirin is suggested in APS with three or more losses, not in unexplained RPL.

options.text: hCG only, because the guideline prefers it to progesterone in luteal insufficiency.
options.why: The guideline considers the evidence insufficient for both progesterone and hCG in luteal insufficiency.

items.explanation: There is evidence that heparin and aspirin do not improve live birth in unexplained RPL; progesterone depends on bleeding in the new pregnancy.

items.stem: What does ESHRE (2022) say about intravenous immunoglobulin in unexplained RPL?

options.text: That they are not recommended in any case (strong), like lymphocyte immunisation or intralipid.
options.why: They are the nuanced exception: the guideline leaves open a possible improvement in a specific group.

options.text: That they are recommended after two unexplained losses (strong), at low monthly doses before conception.
options.why: The group, strength and regimen are incorrect.

options.text: That they can be considered if blood NK cells are raised, regardless of the number of losses.
options.why: The guideline does not link their use to NK cells, whose testing it considers unsupported.

options.text: That repeated high doses very early may improve live birth with four or more losses (conditional).
options.why: Correct: conditional, ⊕⊕○○, based on a single high-quality RCT and calling for more trials.

items.explanation: Outside RPL, NICE says not to use immunological agents, including immunoglobulins, in fertility treatment (1.42.1).

items.stem: In unexplained RPL, which statement about immunotherapies is correct according to ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: G-CSF is not recommended (strong, ⊕⊕⊕○): a large high-quality trial showed no benefit.
options.why: Correct: the Eapen (2019) trial outweighs the earlier smaller trial.

options.text: Prednisolone is recommended (conditional), because its adverse effects are negligible.
options.why: Glucocorticoids are not recommended (strong): there is some signal of benefit, but adverse effects weigh.

options.text: Intralipid can be considered (conditional), because its safety is well established.
options.why: Intralipid is not recommended (strong), because of insufficient evidence.

options.text: Lymphocyte immunisation can be considered in secondary RPL, without relevant adverse effects.
options.why: It is not recommended (strong) and may have serious adverse effects.

items.explanation: There is no evidence for endometrial scratching in RPL (GPP); the only immunotherapy the guideline leaves open is immunoglobulin in a specific group.

items.stem: A woman with RPL (fictional case) asks whether she should take vitamin D and a multivitamin. What does ESHRE (2022) say?

options.text: Measure vitamin D and treat deficiency with high doses, because it prevents the next loss (strong).
options.why: The guideline does not attribute a proven preventive effect to vitamin D: evidence of efficacy is lacking.

options.text: Advise against both, because any supplement in pregnancy increases the risk of loss.
options.why: The guideline does not advise against them: vitamin D can be suggested and safe multivitamins advised.

options.text: Vitamin D can be suggested (evidence is lacking) and, if asked, safe multivitamins, not as treatment.
options.why: Correct: both are GPP.

options.text: Multivitamins as treatment for unexplained RPL (conditional) and vitamin D only if PCOS is present.
options.why: Multivitamins are not presented as treatment, and vitamin D is not conditional on PCOS.

items.explanation: Supplements are handled as part of preconception counselling, not as treatment for RPL.

items.stem: On weight and metformin in RPL, which statement is correct according to ESHRE (2022)?

options.text: Metformin in pregnancy is recommended in all RPL with insulin resistance, to reduce loss (strong).
options.why: It is not recommended, because of insufficient evidence (conditional).

options.text: Obesity and significant underweight are linked to obstetric complications; metformin in pregnancy is not recommended.
options.why: Correct: the first is strong; metformin is not recommended for insufficient evidence in RPL with glucose metabolism alterations (conditional).

options.text: Weight does not influence RPL, so lifestyle advice is limited to stopping smoking and alcohol.
options.why: The guideline includes obesity, alcohol and excessive exercise in lifestyle advice.

options.text: Underweight protects against loss, so keeping a slightly below-normal BMI is advised.
options.why: Invented claim: significant underweight is associated with complications and a normal weight is advised.

items.explanation: ESHRE advises stopping smoking, a normal weight, limiting alcohol and normal exercise (GPP).

items.stem: Among the supportive care elements valued in the ESHRE RPL guideline, which is correct?

options.text: Use technical terms such as “habitual abortion” or “products” to avoid ambiguity.
options.why: The guideline asks precisely to avoid such terms.

options.text: Reassure by promising that the next pregnancy will go well, to reduce anxiety.
options.why: The guideline asks for honesty without false promises.

options.text: Clear, sensitive language, using the patient's own terms, and early scans if she wishes.
options.why: Correct: together with time for questions, listening, respect, honesty and shared planning.

options.text: Focus care only on the woman, because men have no support needs of their own.
options.why: The guideline notes that data on men are lacking and their support preferences may differ.

items.explanation: There is no single model of supportive care; the elements listed by the guideline are text, not graded recommendations.

items.stem: The ESHRE RPL guideline cites a study in which the odds ratio for moderate or severe depression in women with RPL was greater than five. What is the correct reading?

options.text: That more than five in ten women with RPL have moderate or severe depression.
options.why: An odds ratio is not a prevalence.

options.text: That depression is exactly five times more frequent, so all women should be treated.
options.why: An odds ratio is not the same as “times more frequent”, and the guideline does not propose treating everyone.

options.text: That stress causes RPL, which is why depressed women lose more pregnancies.
options.why: There is no evidence that stress directly causes loss.

options.text: That the odds of depression are much higher in RPL (not the same as a five-fold frequency): psychosocial needs must be attended to.
options.why: Correct: the guideline asks for these needs to be considered; data on men are lacking.

items.explanation: The repeated nature of loss can intensify grief; the guideline asks for care to be organised around the couple's psychosocial needs.

items.stem: A clinic's model gives only a 30% live birth rate per transfer for a couple (fictional case) with two transfers and no positive test. Using the ESHRE RIF document's method, what is most appropriate?

options.text: Compute 1 − 0.7² = 51% using the live birth rate directly: below 60%, another transfer.
options.why: The formula uses the pregnancy rate; if only live birth is available, it is estimated by multiplying by 1.16.

options.text: Estimate the pregnancy rate (30% × 1.16 ≈ 34.8%): 1 − 0.652² ≈ 57%, below 60%, so another transfer.
options.why: Correct: with a third transfer the predicted cumulative probability would exceed 60% (≈ 72%).

options.text: Diagnose RIF, because the document sets the threshold at two failed transfers for everyone.
options.why: The document precisely avoids a fixed number of transfers for everyone.

options.text: Diagnose RIF, because with 34.8% pregnancy per transfer two attempts already add up to 70%.
options.why: Probabilities do not add: 1 − 0.652² ≈ 57%.

items.explanation: The formula is 1 − (1 − PR)ⁿ; if the model only gives live birth, the pregnancy rate can be estimated by multiplying it by 1.16.

items.stem: Why did the ESHRE working group set the RIF threshold at a 60% predicted cumulative probability rather than 95%?

options.text: Because 95% is only reached with donor oocytes and most patients use their own.
options.why: This is not the document's reason: the problem is that very few patients reach 95%.

options.text: Because an RCT compared both thresholds and 60% gave more live births.
options.why: No such RCT exists; the threshold is a good practice decision of the group.

options.text: Because 95% would be useful in research, but very few patients reach it in practice.
options.why: Correct: 60% was chosen as the most useful to guide clinical practice.

options.text: Because 60% equals three transfers in every patient, which simplifies the calculation.
options.why: The number of transfers adding up to 60% varies with each patient's prognosis.

items.explanation: The model should consider at least age, euploidy if tested, and the number of embryos or blastocysts transferred.

items.stem: In a couple with RIF, which of these measures is classified as “recommended” by the ESHRE working group?

options.text: Karyotyping of both partners, despite the low prevalence.
options.why: It can be considered, despite the low prevalence of abnormalities.

options.text: Systematic hysteroscopy before the next transfer cycle.
options.why: It can be considered, especially if ultrasound suggests an abnormality.

options.text: Testing thyroid function and mid-luteal progesterone.
options.why: Both are listed as “can be considered”.

options.text: Review and optimise the lifestyle of both partners.
options.why: Correct: reassessing endometrial thickness is also recommended.

items.explanation: Little is recommended: lifestyle, endometrial thickness, genetic counselling and PGT if there is a chromosomal abnormality, and antiphospholipids if there are additional thrombophilia risk factors.

items.stem: In RIF, which of these tests is listed as “not recommended” by the ESHRE working group?

options.text: Uterine or vaginal microbiome testing.
options.why: Correct: together with NK cells, uterine T cells, cytokines, HLA-C, mitochondrial DNA, sperm FISH and DNA fragmentation.

options.text: 3D ultrasound if not done before.
options.why: It can be considered.

options.text: Testing for chronic endometritis.
options.why: It can be considered, with antibiotics if diagnosed.

options.text: Antiphospholipids without risk factors.
options.why: They can be considered; with additional risk factors they are recommended.

items.explanation: Nor are there sufficient data to routinely recommend a commercial endometrial receptivity test or measuring or treating vitamin D.

items.stem: Which interventions does the ESHRE working group consider (rather than reject) in RIF?

options.text: Endometrial scratching and intrauterine G-CSF.
options.why: Both are “not recommended” in RIF.

options.text: PGT-A and blastocyst transfer.
options.why: Correct: these are the only two in the interventions section that the document considers.

options.text: Low molecular weight heparin and intralipid.
options.why: Both are “not recommended” in RIF.

options.text: Assisted hatching and GnRH agonist pretreatment.
options.why: Both are “not recommended” in RIF.

items.explanation: If a cause is identified (thyroid, APS, uterine malformation, endometriosis or adenomyosis), the corresponding guideline should be followed.

items.stem: In RIF, the meta-analysis of RCTs on PGT-A gave live birth RR 0.98 (95% CI 0.32–2.94). How is it interpreted, together with the rest of the evidence summarised by ESHRE?

options.text: That it reduces live birth to a third, according to the lower limit of the interval.
options.why: The interval crosses 1: it does not demonstrate a reduction.

options.text: That it triples live birth, according to the upper limit, and that is why it is recommended.
options.why: The interval crosses 1, and the document only considers it.

options.text: That it is definitive proof that it does not work, so the document classifies it as “not recommended”.
options.why: Such a wide interval is imprecise, not definitive, and the document considers it.

options.text: That it showed no more live births, although retrospective studies suggest it reduces the number of transfers.
options.why: Correct: that is why the document considers it, without recommending it.

items.explanation: Heparin in RIF did not improve live birth either (RR 1.38; 95% CI 0.64–2.96; 2 RCTs; 71 patients) and is not recommended.

items.stem: A couple with RIF (fictional case) asks for sperm DNA fragmentation testing because “it is recommended for recurrent pregnancy loss”. What is correct?

options.text: Do it, because the RPL guideline strongly recommends it and the population is equivalent.
options.why: In RPL it is conditional, and RPL and RIF are not interchangeable populations.

options.text: The RPL guideline leaves it as an option (conditional, ⊕⊕⊕○), but the RIF document does not recommend it.
options.why: Correct: check which population each recommendation refers to.

options.text: Both documents recommend it, but only if semen analysis is abnormal.
options.why: The RIF document does not recommend it, and the RPL guideline does not make it conditional on semen analysis.
